title: Stoichiometric silicon-carbide fiber and composites at general industrial cost

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a continuous, scalable route to near-stoichiometric silicon-carbide (SiC) fiber that preserves demanding high-temperature performance while making its composites economical across a broad range of structural applications. Near-stoichiometric means that the fiber composition approaches the silicon-to-carbon proportions of SiC. The central advance would be in precursor chemistry and fiber manufacturing: producing useful reinforcement consistently, affordably and in sufficient volume.

High-performance near-stoichiometric fibers already exist. The January 2024 article abstract describes small-diameter fibers meeting the property requirements of most ceramic-matrix composite (CMC) and nuclear applications. The proposed breakthrough therefore concerns economical production and deployment of an established useful material class. Its full scope includes finished composites: inexpensive fiber would accomplish only part of the goal if manufacturing those fibers into qualified structural parts remained prohibitively expensive.

significance.text: Fiber cost is a documented major obstacle to broader use. The January 2024 abstract attributes more than 50% of the cost of a finished SiC-fiber CMC part to its fiber and describes fiber manufacturing cost as prohibitively high for applications requiring lower costs. Reducing that contribution while retaining performance could substantially improve finished-part economics. The 2023 DOE project poster identifies prospective demand spanning jet engines and many other high-temperature products, motivated by performance, efficiency and emissions goals.

Conditional synthesis: if economical fiber also enabled economical finished parts, high-temperature CMC structures could become practical in substantially more applications. Greater production volume could then support broader supplier availability and more routine manufacturing. These downstream possibilities depend on composite fabrication, qualification, reliability and service performance; fiber price is a major barrier, but the supplied evidence does not establish it as the sole barrier.

Interpretive analogy: the potential revolution resembles the expansion of structural possibilities associated with inexpensive mass-produced steel—a change in access, scale and economic choice. This is an analogy rather than a documented forecast or a claim that SiC composites could replace steel across ordinary structures. Nor would cheaper fiber itself establish a higher oxidation limit. A large percentage reduction in manufacturing cost would be consequential, but would establish this broader innovation only if the resulting material and finished parts became economically attractive in the intended applications.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is an integrated precursor and manufacturing route that delivers near-stoichiometric SiC fiber with demanding high-temperature properties at commercially useful output and substantially improved economics. The 2023 poster identifies batch processing and legacy manufacturing technology that is difficult to scale as cost drivers. The January 2024 abstract calls for an alternative SiC fiber precursor to lower cost. Together, these sources establish a historical manufacturing and affordability challenge; they do not establish whether the complete capability remains unavailable in November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: a successful route must reconcile precursor affordability, continuous processing, compositional control and preservation of fiber performance. Increasing throughput is insufficient if the resulting fiber loses strength or application-relevant creep or fatigue resistance. Conversely, producing an excellent laboratory tow does not resolve manufacturing yield, consistent quality, sustained output or unit economics. These are concrete requirements implied by the proposed innovation, rather than individually demonstrated failure mechanisms in the supplied review.

Engineering synthesis: the manufacturing advance must also survive integration into finished composites. Fiber savings need to remain meaningful after composite fabrication and qualification, and the resulting parts must perform under their intended temperatures, loads and environments. The supplied evidence does not provide a complete cost breakdown beyond the reported majority contribution from fiber, so it cannot establish how much total cost would fall or which remaining process would become the dominant constraint.

current_state.text: Soydan Ozcan and Sefa Yilmaz’s DOE AMMTO/IEDO peer-review poster, presented on 16–18 May 2023 under contract CPS 38171, describes a project intended to supply domestic, open-market SiC fiber meeting performance, production-volume and affordability needs. According to the supplied review, the poster reports intermediate process achievements and identifies further scale-up work and techno-economic analysis. It does not establish a completed commercial demonstration. The review had an untruncated text extraction of the poster; the evidence summarized here does not depend on additional inspection of its graphics.

The poster states a SiC fiber cost of $10,000/kg and anticipates an approximately 80–90% manufacturing-cost reduction. Applying that percentage to the stated baseline gives an illustrative $1,000–$2,000/kg. This calculation is neither a measured production cost nor a commercial selling price: the baseline comes from a project document rather than an audited price series, and the percentage is an expected manufacturing improvement. The supplied evidence also does not establish whether that calculated range would necessarily confine the material to specialty applications; that judgment requires application-specific finished-part economics.

Sefa Yilmaz, Merlin Theodore and Soydan Ozcan’s article, “Silicon carbide fiber manufacturing: Cost and technology,” appeared in Composites Part B, volume 269, article 111101, dated 15 January 2024. Its abstract reports useful near-stoichiometric small-diameter fibers, identifies manufacturing cost as prohibitively high, and attributes more than half of finished SiC-fiber CMC part cost to fiber. The supplied source is the ORNL publication landing page and abstract, rather than the full article. Its available text supports these statements but does not supply detailed cost models or numerical performance acceptance thresholds.

The supplied evidence documents the motivation and partial progress in 2023–2024. It does not establish a later audited commercial price, sustained commercial output or broad cost-based adoption by November 2026. The supplied freshness record contains no search entries, so it cannot support the earlier assertion that a search found no later price. Present-day availability remains unresolved; this evidence limitation establishes neither achievement nor continued nonachievement.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a commercial-scale route producing near-stoichiometric SiC fiber that matches a specified aerospace-grade reference in strength and application-relevant creep or fatigue performance. The reference fiber, composition requirements, operating temperatures, loads, environments and test durations should be specified before comparison. These are proposed criteria for assessing this innovation, not established industry thresholds supplied by the sources.
completion_criteria.label: Commercial-scale near-stoichiometric SiC fiber matches aerospace-grade reference performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic demonstration: report measured production output and fiber economics alongside the economics of representative finished composites. Distinguish manufacturing cost from selling price, and explain production scale, yield and other assumptions that materially affect the comparison. Convincing completion would include manufacturers selecting the composites for a broad class of high-temperature structural parts on cost as well as required performance. A laboratory tow or projected percentage reduction alone would not meet that scope. No universal dollar-per-kilogram cutoff is proposed.
completion_criteria.label: Measured fiber-to-composite economics support broad manufacturer selection on cost

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary demonstration: show consistent composition, properties, output and economics across repeated production campaigns, with independent performance verification where practical. Demonstrate finished parts in several representative service conditions and identify the applications for which the economic and performance case holds. A finite demonstration establishes breadth within those tested conditions; it cannot establish universal suitability across all high-temperature structures.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatable production results and finished-part tests establish application boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRM-02, “Load-bearing ceramics that survive long service in air above the silica limit,” addresses environmental durability at a higher service-temperature boundary. CRM-08 addresses economical fiber production and composite access. Lower cost does not itself establish survival above the silica limit, while improved environmental durability would not itself establish affordable fiber. The roster titles support this broad distinction, but fuller definitions are needed to specify their exact material and operating boundaries.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-11, “Net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics,” concerns shaping and densification, whereas CRM-08 centers on precursor chemistry, fiber manufacture and composite economics. Shaping improvements could complement cheaper reinforcement by reducing finished-part costs, but the roster does not establish that CRM-11 covers continuous-fiber CMC processing. Their relationship therefore cannot be restricted confidently to a particular shared manufacturing step.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-07, “A low-activation structural ceramic that keeps its heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation,” concerns irradiation-dependent service properties. The reported suitability of existing fibers for many nuclear applications does not demonstrate preservation of heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation. Affordable SiC fiber could be complementary where such reinforcement is useful, but CRM-08 does not establish CRM-07’s specialized performance capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-01’s room-temperature tensile ductility, CRM-05’s repeated restoration of strength after critical cracks and CRM-12’s near-theoretical failure stress in large transparent ceramics each concern distinct mechanical or functional achievements. Broadly affordable SiC reinforcement would not, by itself, demonstrate any of them. CRM-04’s elimination of a high-temperature furnace cycle could offer a separate route to lower ceramic processing costs, but CRM-08 does not require furnace-free manufacture. These remain separate innovations with potentially complementary benefits.

unresolved_issues: Whether commercial production meeting CRM-08’s combined performance, volume and affordability scope exists as of November 2026 remains unestablished.
Realized costs, selling prices, sustained output and finished-part economics following the 2023 project require evidence beyond the supplied materials.
The supplied review does not detail the poster’s intermediate process achievements sufficiently to report their quantitative performance.
The full 2024 article was not available in the reviewed evidence; its detailed methods and cost analysis cannot be inferred from the abstract.
The reference fiber, performance thresholds, operating conditions and breadth of applications for a convincing completion demonstration remain to be specified.
Exact relationships with CRM-02 and CRM-11 remain limited by the absence of full concept definitions; the supplied roster supports only the broad distinctions adopted here.

brief.title: Affordable heat-resistant fibers and parts
possible: Manufacturers could use affordable, heat-resistant parts in more jet engines, power turbines and other demanding equipment. These parts would use silicon carbide fibers, made of silicon and carbon, to reinforce ceramics. The combined materials are called composites.

A continuous manufacturing process would supply these fibers in large quantities while keeping silicon and carbon close to the required proportions. The goal is affordable finished parts that retain their strength under heat and load.
why: Fiber accounts for more than half the cost of a finished silicon carbide composite part. Making it cheaper would remove a major obstacle to wider use.
Broader access to these materials would give engine and energy-equipment manufacturers more options for lightweight structures that withstand extreme heat, supporting efficiency and emissions goals.

sources.who: Soydan Ozcan, Sefa Yilmaz and collaborators at Oak Ridge National Laboratory
sources.showed: The team installed a prototype fiber production line and demonstrated continuous heat treatment. It also hardened starting fibers at a rate suitable for commercial manufacturing.
sources.quote:
A prototype SiC Fiber line was installed and commissioned at Carbon Fiber Technology Facility
(CFTF) in Oak Ridge National Labs.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates steps toward continuous fiber manufacturing that could expand to commercial output.
sources.not_established: The prototype does not establish sustained commercial output, measured production costs or affordable finished parts.

sources.who: Sefa Yilmaz, Merlin Theodore and Soydan Ozcan
sources.showed: They reported that existing fibers meet the requirements of most ceramic composite and nuclear applications. Their analysis identified preparation of raw materials and hardening of starting fibers as expensive manufacturing steps.
sources.quote: Analysis of the existing polycarbosilane (PCS)-based SiC fiber manufacturing shows that the crosslinking (curing) and raw material preparation steps are high-cost steps that need lower cost options.
sources.cited_for: Useful fibers already exist, but manufacturing cost prevents broader use.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not demonstrate a cheaper commercial process that preserves performance or makes finished composites broadly economical.

shown: High-performance silicon carbide fibers already exist. Oak Ridge National Laboratory and its partners demonstrated parts of a continuous manufacturing process, including a prototype line. Their projected savings remain expectations, rather than measured commercial costs.
missing: A commercial-scale process must demonstrate the required composition and heat-resistant performance together with sustained output.
Measured fiber and finished-part economics must support broad use by manufacturers.
Repeated production and finished-part testing must establish consistent quality and the conditions in which the parts work.

milestones.label: Commercial fibers match aerospace reference performance
milestones.explanation: Commercial production would have to match a specified aerospace fiber in strength and resistance to slow deformation or repeated loading. This would show that scaling production preserves performance.

milestones.label: Measured costs make composites a broad manufacturing choice
milestones.explanation: Measured output, fiber costs and prices, and finished-part economics would have to support broad manufacturer selection on cost and performance. This would establish affordability beyond projected fiber savings.

milestones.label: Repeated production and part tests establish application boundaries
milestones.explanation: Repeated production would have to deliver consistent quality, output and economics, with finished parts tested under several service conditions. This would establish where the performance and cost advantages hold.

uncertain: Whether commercial production already combines the required performance, output and affordability remains unresolved.
The reference fiber, test conditions and performance thresholds for judging success remain to be specified.
How broadly finished parts would become economical depends on fabrication and qualification costs as well as fiber savings.

page.title: Continuous near-stoichiometric SiC fiber manufacture
page.definition: Continuous production supplies silicon carbide (SiC) fiber at DOE’s US$1,500/kg fiber-cost target for reinforcement in ceramics. Near-stoichiometric means approximately one silicon atom per carbon atom.

goal.need: A 2024 review reports that near-stoichiometric SiC fibers already meet the property requirements of most ceramic-matrix-composite and nuclear applications. It attributes more than 50% of finished SiC-fiber composite part cost to fiber, making fiber manufacture a majority contribution to address.

statements.quote: Alternative SiC fiber precursor should be sought for lowering the cost of SiC fibers.

statements.body: DOE Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office project CPS 38171

statements.quote: Overall, the high cost of CMC products blocks the wider use of these materials, especially for ‚cost-sensitive‘ applications.
statements.context: CMC means ceramic-matrix composite; the statement concerns finished components.

completion.title: Continuous SiC-fiber manufacture meets DOE’s US$1,500/kg fiber-cost target.
completion.criterion: Produce near-stoichiometric SiC fiber continuously through a domestic supply chain at a fiber cost of at most US$1,500/kg, with 500+ filament tows meeting required tensile strength and modulus, at a rate scalable to >5,000 kg/year per commercial line. Numerical mechanical acceptance limits and the cost-accounting boundary are unspecified.
completion.set_by: DOE AMMTO, CPS 38171 poster: Current/Target table and End Project Goal. The dollar threshold appears only in the table.
completion.basis: DOE supplies a numerical fiber-manufacturing target. Finished-composite affordability remains application-specific; ASTM C1835 is a classification rather than a complete material specification. General Atomics’ paper published on 17 March 2026 reports cost reductions of up to 60% for some manufacturing steps, which does not establish the total fiber-cost target.

milestones.title: SiC precursor fibers undergo continuous, in-line devitrification.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate roll-to-roll devitrification, the crystallization of glassy precursor fibers. Reported in May 2023 in a programme poster; not journal peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DOE AMMTO/ORNL, CPS 38171 poster, Key Achievements: published process demonstration.

milestones.title: A pilot process produces more than 1 kg of SiC fiber per day.
milestones.criterion: Produce >1 kg/day of SiC fiber at ORNL’s Carbon Fiber Technology Facility.
milestones.set_by: DOE AMMTO/ORNL, CPS 38171 poster, Technology Transfer target.

milestones.title: Continuous manufacture makes 500+ filament SiC tows at rates scalable to >5,000 kg/year per line.
milestones.criterion: Continuously manufacture a SiC tow, a filament bundle, meeting the programme’s filament-count, tensile-property and annual-capacity requirements stated in the completion criterion. Capacity is a scale-up requirement, not demonstrated annual output.
milestones.set_by: DOE AMMTO/ORNL, CPS 38171 poster, End Project Goal.

not_found: No universal finished-composite affordability threshold was found in the DOE, ASTM, NASA or Composites United material searched.
Numerical mechanical and composition acceptance limits, and cost-accounting rules for CPS 38171, were not located.
No published result jointly establishing the programme’s production, mechanical-property and total fiber-cost targets was found.
The full 2024 cost paper could not be opened at OSTI or ScienceDirect.
